doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Elvin Jones and fellow drummers, and Philly Joe Jones
summary: He admired Elvin's crossed rhythms, valued every drummer's own approach, and denies a rift with Philly Joe, whom he befriended in New York.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: The business. Well let’s go back to listening to the John Coltrane quartet. What was your impression? I mean you probably heard Elvin before that.

Oh, yeah, man. I was very impressed with Elvin, man. Elvin did things man, nobody else could do. He’d played (unintelligible) rhythms as they call them, whatever, he crossed rhythms man. I remember hearing him one time man; they’re playing a ballad, right. All of a sudden man, old thunder (unintelligible), man he played some that was just -- you talking about out of left field, I mean -- and came back in. Goddamn, it worked. But to hear, I mean all of sudden, you know. Elvin was something else man. Well I was close with all my contemporary drummers, man. You know, always had affection towards, an appreciation -- everybody was doing -- because everybody was doing something different. I didn’t try to play like Max or Elvin, I couldn’t, you know, and they didn’t play like me. Everybody did their own thing, which was cool.
There was a CD that you had yesterday where it starts out talking about how Philly Joe Jones, that you were -­
Yeah, that’s what I figured but I wanted to make sure you could clarify -­
No, man, some English guy wrote that. It really ticked me off when I read it.
But you were cool with Philly Joe Jones?
Oh, yeah, Philly and I were -­
Because you probably ran into him in England too.
No, man, I ran into Philly when I first came to New York man. He was on his back He used to come out and hang out with me every night, man. He was something else man. We were cool.
